title: Mary's falling asleep (15 August)
hookLine: Orthodox keep the Dormition, Catholics the Assumption; many Protestants simply honor Mary as a faithful disciple

lines: AN ICON: A WOMAN ON A BIER.
JESUS HOLDS HER SOUL LIKE A CHILD.
SHE CARRIED HIM. NOW HE CARRIES HER.
cards: Here is an Orthodox icon. A woman lies on a bier, eyes closed, hands folded. The apostles crowd around her, some bending close, some weeping.
Behind it stands Jesus, in light, holding a tiny figure wrapped in white, like a newborn. It's her soul. At the start of the Gospels, she carried him as a baby.
In this picture, he carries her. The woman is Mary, the mother of Jesus. Orthodox Christians call this moment her falling asleep.

teach.h: BEHOLD THE HANDMAID OF THE LORD.
teach.b: In Luke, her answer to the angel ends in a yes: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word."
At the cross, in John, Jesus gives her into a disciple's care: "Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home."
The last time Acts names her, she is praying with the apostles: "Mary the mother of Jesus." After that, silence. The New Testament never tells how her life ended.
So the churches keep this day in three ways. Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition, which means falling asleep.
The New Testament can speak of the faithful dead as sleeping; of Stephen, stoned in Acts, the King James says simply, "he fell asleep."
The Orthodox tradition holds that Mary truly died, surrounded by the apostles, that her Son received her soul, as the icon shows, and that her body too was then taken up to heaven.
Catholics keep the fifteenth of August as the Assumption: Catholic teaching holds that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into the glory of heaven.

teach.h: SCRIPTURE IS SILENT ON HER DEATH.
teach.b: Protestants who don't hold either as a teaching give a plain reason: scripture doesn't tell the story.
They honor her as Luke does, the faithful disciple who said yes all the way to the cross and the upper room, and some keep the day as a festival of Mary.
What all three share is the woman in Luke who said, "all generations shall call me blessed," and a sense that the one who carried Jesus was not forgotten by him.

how: Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition of Mary in August, and Catholics keep the Assumption on the fifteenth; some Protestant churches keep a festival of Mary, and others simply remember her as a faithful disciple.

games.q: you're the disciple at the foot of the cross. Jesus says to you, behold thy mother. what do you do?
o: stay with her until it's over, then go home alone.

games.why: John says that from that hour the disciple took her unto his own home.

practice: Think of a woman who carried someone, a mother, a grandmother, a neighbor who raised half the street, and of one thing she did again and again without applause: a packed lunch, a light left on.
If you pray, thank God for her by name; if you don't, hold her with thanks. If she has died, you might picture her as the icon does, being carried now.

wordCard.voice: Dormition. The falling asleep of Mary, the Orthodox name for the end of her earthly life. Catholics keep the feast as the Assumption.

orig.note: Greek: a falling asleep. the Orthodox name for the feast, given in modern Greek pronunciation; Latin dormitio.
